newsitem.title: UK: CLEANER CAR GAINS SEEN SWAMPED BY ASIA MANIA.
newsitem.headline: CLEANER CAR GAINS SEEN SWAMPED BY ASIA MANIA.

text.p: By Neil Winton, Science and Technology Correspondent
Car mania in Asia and Latin America threatens to swamp any gains made in protecting the world from automobile pollution.

Most new petrol-powered cars no longer pump out killer gases, although they still spew ever-increasing amounts of carbon dioxide, the main greenhouse gas. But all this progress is threatened by an explosion of car ownership over the next 10 years in new markets.

World leaders, meeting at the United Nations in New York last week to discuss progress made since the Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro in 1992, hinted that, if the environment is to be protected, a firm grip must be taken on the ubiquitous automobile.

"Worldwide there's going to be a problem because there are just too many cars coming. If China, with one billion people, is getting interested on any sort of scale there will be many, many cars," said Rudolf Rijkeboer, transport engineer at the TNO Institute in Delft, Netherlands.
FORECASTS POINT TO CAR GROWTH EXPLOSION
Forecasts of the number of cars on the world's roads next century vary wildly, but they all agree on one thing: growth will be explosive.

German luxury car and truck maker Mercedes said at a recent conference that the world's car fleet, having risen from about 700 million in 1990 to 800 million in 1995, would explode to 1.6 billion by 2030.
Michael Walsh, automobile industry consultant from Arlington, Virginia, reckons there will be between 1.1 billion and 1.2 billion cars on the roads, and tracks, of the world by 2010.

Experts hope that all these new vehicles will at least adopt the clean technology of the West, where about 90 percent of gasoline cars produced last year were fitted with catalytic convertors. This severely cuts emissions of carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons, and oxides of nitrogen (NOX).

Some experts say that the automobile can be made almost environmentally neutral with new technologies such as hybrid combinations of diesel and battery engines, and eventually the hydrogen-powered fuel cell which emits only water.
Others say this is all hopelessly utopian, at least in the short term. But there is still huge potential to make current vehicles more efficient by up to 40 percent.
"This whole field is riddled with technical fantasies," said Dr Steve Cousins, transport and automotive specialist at Britain's Cranfield University.

Telematics, where computers are used to marshall traffic and eventually may take over driving vehicles, is another blind alley. This would just make it easier to travel longer distances and consume more carbon dioxide, Cousins said.
SCOPE TO IMPROVE TECHNOLOGY

"We are getting rid of bad polluting cars as new models replace old ones. You can do so much more with existing technologies. And just organising traffic in cities more intelligently promises big dividends," said Cousins.
Michael Walsh agrees.

"New materials to lower weight, better aerodynamics, more effective transmissions, better air conditioning, generally more efficient vehicles will save resources, but CO2 (carbon dioxide) is still a problem even with catalytic convertors," he said.
Conventional methods have great scope, said TNO's Rijkeboer.

"Fuel cells and the like will help, but I don't see a great market yet for that sort of thing. The major impact at the moment should come from conventional technology, making vehicles light, then engines can be smaller, there's still a lot of improvement possible from aerodynamics," he said.
"You can save about 40 percent of current fuel with thoughtful improvement."
But according to experts, consumers show little sign so far that will get their cheque books out for fuel efficient, environmentally friendly cars.
Threatened higher taxes on cars and car use may price some of the poor off the road, but raising the costs of motoring is only likely to raise funds for governments, not curb car use.
Rijkeboer said more direct government action might be necessary. He suggests a mandatory maximum fuel consumption which car manufacturers would have to match.
According to Walsh, there is an underlying threat to the planet which must be addressed, or else.

"We are at a critical juncture. Between now and the meeting in Kyoto, Japan in December, industrialised countries have to make firm commitments concerning CO2 from the transportation sector," said Walsh.
The United Nations' Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change meeting in Kyoto is charged with setting mandatory limits on national emissions of greenhouse gases.

The European Union may seek a cut of 15 percent in emmissions below 1990 levels by 2010. The United States has made it clear it is unhappy about mandatory limits and has suggested a system of carbon credits which could be traded on markets.
Any agreement will be greeted with a degree of cynicism as the Rio Earth Summit target of cutting carbon dioxide to 1990 levels by 2000 will be hopelessly missed by most industrialised countries.
The time for action is approaching, Walsh said, because fossil fuel is finite, although projections that there are only 40 years supply left have been made for the last 40 years.
"If we use up all of this precious commodity it will take a very long time for that carbon to go away, for us to return the atmosphere to what it was in pre-industrial times," said Walsh.
"Meantime, there is a growing body of evidence that we are in global warming already, which we are in danger of exacerbating while squandering this assett."
